Vernal

VER-nuhl · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vernal is relating to spring, or having the fresh, youthful qualities associated with springtime.

The vernal equinox, when day and night are of equal length, marks the official start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere.

Worked Example

There was something almost vernal about her mood that morning -- a sudden lightness and hope, like the first warm day after a long winter.

Vernal describes anything relating to spring, or carrying spring's fresh, renewing, youthful qualities -- here, used figuratively to describe a person's sudden burst of hope.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

springlike: Springlike describes how something feels — mild air, bright light, a hopeful morning can all be springlike whatever the calendar says. Vernal is the formal word for what actually belongs to spring, as in the vernal equinox, and it can also carry spring's fresh, youthful mood in writing.

budding: Budding is about stage, not season: a budding friendship or a budding talent is just starting to grow, like a plant pushing out its first buds. Vernal ties a thing to spring itself, or to spring's fresh and hopeful mood, rather than to how new it is.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

wintry: cold and bleak, like winter

autumnal: relating to fall, often suggesting decline or fading

Where it sits · how vividly new growth shows through — mild → vernal → blossoming

mild vs. vernal: Something mild is simply not harsh, without vernal's specific link to spring's renewal and new growth.

blossoming vs. vernal: Something blossoming is bursting fully into bloom, an even more vivid image of spring's growth than the more general vernal.

Build the Word

The pieces

root (limited family) — vern-

root (limited family) — vern-: spring -- from Latin ver, a root that produced very few other common English words (Latin ver)

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: relating to, characteristic of (Latin (-alis))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ver ('spring') plus the adjective ending -al ('relating to') -- vernal simply means 'relating to spring.' It is not related to the similar-looking word vernacular, which grows from a completely different Latin root.

Sounds related -- but isn't: vernacular

Sounds related -- but isn't: vernacular: Vernacular looks like vernal with extra letters, but it grows from a completely different Latin root -- only vernal carries ver, 'spring.' And ver produced very few other common English words, so vernal is close to a one-word family.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Vernal appears often in formal or scientific contexts (vernal equinox, vernal pool) but can also be used more poetically for anything with spring's fresh, hopeful, youthful quality. Be careful not to confuse it with the unrelated word vernacular.
